settings.heading: Experience The Next Level Of Hearing
settings.text: Getting news that your newborn has congenital hearing loss can feel overwhelming and confusing.

settings.title: Genetic factors
settings.text: About half of congenital cases have a genetic explanation. Examples include mutations like GJB2 (connexin 26) and SLC26A4 (pendrin).

settings.title: Infections during pregnancy
settings.text: Rubella, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and toxoplasmosis can affect fetal hearing development.

settings.title: Birth complications
settings.text: Prematurity, low birth weight, or oxygen deprivation at birth can contribute.

settings.title: Ototoxic exposure
settings.text: Certain medications and toxins can damage the inner ear.

settings.heading: What Is Congenital Hearing Loss?
settings.description:
Congenital hearing loss means a baby is born with—or develops during pregnancy—a degree of hearing loss. It can affect one ear (unilateral) or both ears (bilateral), and that distinction matters for how we plan care and support.


Important note: Bilateral hearing loss (both ears) usually has a bigger impact on language development than unilateral loss, so it often requires quicker intervention.

settings.title: OAE (Otoacoustic Emissions)
settings.desc: OAE checks how the cochlea (inner ear) responds to sound. It’s quick, painless, and widely used for newborn screening.

settings.title: ABR (Auditory Brainstem Response)
settings.desc: ABR measures electrical activity in the auditory nerve and brainstem in response to sounds. It's useful when OAE results are abnormal or when there’s a higher neurological risk.

settings.title: ASSR (Auditory Steady-State Response)
settings.desc: ASSR gives frequency-specific estimates of hearing thresholds, which helps audiologists determine how much amplification a child needs at different pitches.

settings.title: Tympanometry
settings.desc: This test assesses middle-ear function—useful for detecting fluid, infection, or eustachian tube issues.

settings.heading: Assessment & Diagnosis: The Tests You Should Know
settings.subtext: A clear diagnosis is the first step to an effective plan. These are the main tests used with newborns and infants:

settings.title: Sensorineural
settings.desc: damage to the cochlea or auditory nerve (often permanent).

settings.title: Conductive
settings.desc: sound isn't transmitted efficiently to the inner ear (often treatable medically or surgically).

settings.title: Mixed
settings.desc: a combination of sensorineural and conductive factors.

settings.title: Mild
settings.desc: Soft sounds are hard to hear.

settings.title: Moderate
settings.desc: Speech can be unclear without help.

settings.title: Severe
settings.desc: Normal conversation is difficult to hear.

settings.title: Profound
settings.desc: Very limited access to sound; often considered for cochlear implant.

settings.heading: How Severe Is It?
settings.subtext: Understanding the different types of hearing loss helps guide the right care for your child.

settings.label: Option 1
settings.title: Hearing Aids
settings.tags: Durable Builds, Speech-focused tuning, Child Friendly Color
settings.desc: Pediatric Behind-The-Ear (BTE) models with replaceable earmolds as your child grows. Brands like Phonak Sky are designed specifically for kids.

settings.label: Option 2
settings.title: Cochlear Implants
settings.tags: Surgical solution, Post-op therapy required, Significant gains possible
settings.desc: For bilateral severe-to-profound hearing loss when hearing aids provide limited benefit. Earlier implantation plus therapy yields better outcomes.

settings.label: Option 3
settings.title: FM Systems
settings.tags: Classroom support, Direct signal transmission, Noise reduction
settings.desc: Remote microphone systems that dramatically improve hearing in noisy environments like classrooms by boosting speech-to-noise ratio.

settings.label: Option 4
settings.title: Speech Therapy
settings.tags: Early start matters, Parent-guided learning, Language-building focus
settings.desc: Language therapy should start ASAP. Parents are the most important "therapists"—talking, reading, and labeling objects throughout the day are powerful ways to build language.

settings.content_text: Being new parents of a child with congenital hearing loss may bring unique challenges, but with the right support and resources, your child can flourish. Early intervention is crucial, so consult professionals for comprehensive evaluations and personalized treatment options like hearing aids or cochlear implants.

settings.tab_title: I'm A Child with Hearing Loss
settings.content_title: I'm A Child with Hearing Loss
settings.content_text: Children can lose hearing during their teenage years, sometimes with very little warning. The causes of hearing loss can differ widely between each child, so do their physiological effects. If left untreated, it can be devastating to teenagers, who are already suffering from social and emotional trials at this time in their life.

settings.tab_title: Hearing Tests for Newborns, Babies, Toddlers and Children
settings.content_title: Hearing Tests for Newborns, Babies, Toddlers and Children
settings.content_text: Hearing tests are crucial for detecting and addressing hearing loss in babies, toddlers, and children. Regular hearing checks should also be conducted to ensure the child's hearing development is on track, and any hearing loss can be detected and addressed promptly.

Your baby needs to hear sounds to learn how to speak and learn about the world. Given that the signs and symptoms of hearing impairment in babies vary, it is quite challenging to detect. Here're some hearing milestones that you can use as a guide for your baby's first 3 years of life.

Teenagers are at a higher risk of hearing loss due to exposure to loud music, frequent use of headphones, and attending noisy social events. By using hearing protection, they can avoid the negative consequences of hearing loss later in life.

settings.tab_title: Protect Your Child's Hearing with Earmuffs
settings.content_title: Protect Your Child's Hearing with Earmuffs
settings.content_text: Children learn from their parents, so it’s important to model the hearing behaviors we want to encourage in our kids. The damaging effect of noise exposure on our hearing is cumulative, so it’s important to protect hearing from an early age. Bring earplugs or ear muffs with you when there is potential for loud noise.
